newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FEATURE - Hong Kong handover leaves Taiwan exposed.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hong Kong handover leaves Taiwan exposed.

text.p: Hong Kong's July 1 return to Chinese rule threatens to shake the territory's role as the main conduit for huge Taiwan investments into China, and it could expose Taiwan to economic coercion from the mainland.
With China as its biggest political adversary but also its top trade partner, Taiwan finds its economy in a precarious position as Beijing prepares to take over Hong Kong.

"I don't think it is in China's interest to use Hong Kong as a hostage to threaten Taiwan, but you can already see the Taiwan government becoming more cautious," said Amy Huang, analyst for Nomura Securities.

Taiwan's investments in Hong Kong are small, but the colony serves as the main transit stop for an estimated US$30 billion in "indirect" investments that Taiwan businesses have poured into China since a late-1980s political thaw. Taiwan still bans direct contacts with the communist mainland.
In 1996, Taiwan approved more than US$1.2 billion in indirect China investments, a 12 percent rise from 1995, and hundreds of millions more flowed in through offshore subsidiaries.
VULNERABLE IN TRADE
Taiwan is particularly vulnerable in trade.
The island's exports to Hong Kong in 1996 stood at US$26.805 billion -- most of it destined for China -- while imports were just US$1.705 billion.
Taiwan's exports to China grew to US$19.148 billion in 1996, while imports from the mainland were a mere US$3.06 billion.
Facing the combined import clout of Hong Kong and China, Taiwan has far more to lose in a trade showdown.

"China will likely to do something to make Taiwan at least squirm a little bit, both economically and politically," said Eric Liu, analyst for National Securities. "But nobody really knows exactly how far China will go."
Of the many question marks in the Taiwan-China ties, one of the most economically crucial and politically-laden involves shipping across the Taiwan Strait.
Under Taiwan's ban on direct contacts, all shipments still must pass through a "third place" -- chiefly Hong Kong.

China, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province since civil war split them in 1949, considers direct links a "domestic" matter, and may be tempted to use Hong Kong's handover to pressure Taiwan to end the 48-year-old ban.
For its part, Taiwan is reluctant to grant unrestricted contacts because of sovereignty concerns.

Instead of accepting true direct shipments across the strait, Taipei wants a transshipment scheme in which shipments may move between Taiwan and China, but cargoes from China remain outside of Taiwan customs for processing and onward shipment.
Despite recent signs of an imminent breakthrough, China has not consented to Taiwan's proposal.
Nor have the sides even negotiated on the continuation of current direct shipping links between Taiwan and Hong Kong -- a lapse that leaves Taiwan shippers and investors nervous.
POLITICAL GAMESMANSHIP
Nomura's Huang said she expected China to approve some form of direct links eventually -- but not before engaging Taiwan in some painful political gamesmanship.
"China is delaying the links as a political gesture, saying to Taiwan that, 'You need me'. But eventually it is not in China's interest to make good on any threats," Huang said.
"Beijing wants to make sure Hong Kong is satisfied politically and prosperous economically. Cutting off Taiwan is not conducive toward either end," she said.
Taipei, trying to protect the island against potential sanctions from China, has repeatedly called for caution and urged its businesses not to become over-dependent on mainland investments.
Taiwan underscored its resolve last week, vowing to ferret out and punish illegal projects in China as well as investments routed clandestinely into China through overseas interests.
Some analysts say the crackdown could backfire if Taiwan businessmen who are determined to make China investments move more and more of their financing offshore to escape Taiwan regulators' reach.
